# Validation

This file shows validation of the library against reference values, computed independently.

**Reproduce:** Build validation.cpp in Release and have /data folder with input and reference files (generated by make_reference_data.py in /scripts). Reference data comes from QuantLib v1.44.

**Conventions:**
T = days / 365; b (cost of carry) = r - q; Vega = ∂V/∂σ; Theta = -∂V/∂T.
Errors are |computed − reference|. The signed errors in B and G are (computed − reference).
## Summary

- European formulas for price and sensitivities match QuantLib within 3 × 10⁻¹³ [180 options].
- American binomial tree (CRR) matches QuantLib's QD+ fixed-point engine within 7.9 × 10⁻⁴ (call) and 7.7 × 10⁻⁴ (put) [180 options, 10,000 steps], and within 8.0 × 10⁻³ (call) and 7.2 × 10⁻³ (put) across 10,000 random options at about 0.44 ms per option on average [1,000 steps, Apple M4].
- European binomial tree (CRR and JR) converges to Black–Scholes at first order: a 10× increase in steps cuts the error 10× (worst error at 10,000 steps: 7.9 × 10⁻⁴ CRR, 1.3 × 10⁻³ JR) [180 options].
- Long-maturity American options converge to the closed-form perpetual price: gap 4.1 × 10⁻³ (call) and 2.3 × 10⁻³ (put) at T = 100 years [10,000 steps].
- Tree delta and gamma converge to the analytic Greeks at first order. Worst error at 5,001 steps: delta 4.6 × 10⁻⁵ (CRR), 3.7 × 10⁻⁵ (JR); gamma 5.9 × 10⁻⁶ (CRR), 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ (JR).


## Option sets

| Set | Options | Used in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grid | 180: every combination of K = 80, 90, 100, 110, 120; T = 30, 182, 365, 1,095 days; σ = 0.15, 0.30, 0.50; (r, q) = (0.05, 0), (0.05, 0.03), (0.02, 0.06); S = 100 | A, B, C, D, E |
| Random | 10,000 drawn uniformly in the same ranges (K 80–120, 30–1,095 days, σ 0.15–0.50, r 0–0.05, q 0–0.06; fixed seed) | D |
| At the money | S = K = 100, T = 1, σ = 0.30, r = b = 0.05 | B, G |
| Perpetual | K = 100, σ = 0.10, r = 0.10, b = 0.02, S = 110 | F |

## A. European formulas vs QuantLib

European analytic put and call prices and sensitivities were compared to QuantLib analytic European engine on 180 options.

| | Price | Delta | Gamma | Vega | Theta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Call, largest error | 3.2e-14 | 2.5e-15 | 1.8e-16 | 5.2e-14 | 2.5e-13 |
| Put, largest error | 4.3e-14 | 2.6e-15 | 1.8e-16 | 5.2e-14 | 3.0e-13 |

The results show agreement to 3.0e-13 at worst, so they can be used as reference in further studies.

## B. Binomial tree convergence (European)

Binomial tree prices for 180 European call options were compared to analytic solution as number of steps increases from 10 to 10000 for both strategies (Cox-Ross-Rubinstein and Jarrow-Rudd).

| Steps | CRR largest | CRR average | JR largest | JR average |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10 | 0.774 | 0.167 | 1.08 | 0.129 |
| 100 | 0.0784 | 0.0163 | 0.107 | 0.0129 |
| 1,000 | 7.85e-3 | 1.55e-3 | 1.10e-2 | 1.42e-3 |
| 10,000 | 7.85e-4 | 1.62e-4 | 1.25e-3 | 1.38e-4 |

At-the-money option's (from the table) convergence was studied in detail across even and odd number of steps from 10 to 5001 (CRR).

| Steps | Signed error | Error × steps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10 | −0.290 | −2.90 |
| 11 | +0.252 | +2.77 |
| 50 | −0.0588 | −2.94 |
| 51 | +0.0539 | +2.75 |
| 100 | −0.0294 | −2.94 |
| 101 | +0.0272 | +2.75 |
| 500 | −5.89e-3 | −2.95 |
| 501 | +5.48e-3 | +2.75 |
| 1,000 | −2.95e-3 | −2.95 |
| 1,001 | +2.74e-3 | +2.75 |
| 5,000 | −5.89e-4 | −2.95 |
| 5,001 | +5.49e-4 | +2.75 |

The results show first-order convergence as 10× increase in number of steps decreases absolute error by roughly 10×. Error × steps stays at approximately the same level (-2.95 for even number of steps, and +2.75 for odd number of steps). The sign of the error alternates between even and odd step counts, because the strike falls exactly on a final node when the step count is even and between two nodes when it is odd

## C. Tree delta and gamma (European)

European delta and gamma read off the first two steps of a lattice (CRR and JR) were compared to analytic solutions across number of steps from 100 to 5001.

| Steps | Tree | Delta largest | Delta average | Gamma largest | Gamma average |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 100 | CRR | 2.13e-3 | 4.21e-4 | 7.10e-4 | 7.86e-5 |
| 1,000 | CRR | 2.10e-4 | 4.30e-5 | 7.03e-5 | 8.09e-6 |
| 1,001 | CRR | 2.34e-4 | 5.21e-5 | 2.46e-5 | 5.24e-6 |
| 5,000 | CRR | 4.43e-5 | 9.36e-6 | 1.41e-5 | 1.54e-6 |
| 5,001 | CRR | 4.60e-5 | 1.00e-5 | 5.92e-6 | 1.13e-6 |
| 100 | JR | 1.66e-3 | 3.81e-4 | 5.62e-4 | 6.79e-5 |
| 1,000 | JR | 1.63e-4 | 4.21e-5 | 4.26e-5 | 7.06e-6 |
| 1,001 | JR | 2.04e-4 | 4.08e-5 | 6.18e-5 | 6.75e-6 |
| 5,000 | JR | 3.53e-5 | 8.17e-6 | 5.07e-6 | 1.34e-6 |
| 5,001 | JR | 3.65e-5 | 8.72e-6 | 1.28e-5 | 1.44e-6 |

The results show first-order convergence as 10× increase in number of steps decreases absolute error by roughly 10×. Gamma's largest error is observed for the 30-day, low-volatility, at-the-money option, where gamma itself is largest. On odd steps (CRR), gamma's error decreases by 2-3× due to a similar effect as in study B.

## D. American options vs QuantLib

American prices from binomial tree (CRR) were compared to QuantLib's QD+ fixed-point engine: 180 options from the grid across 1000 and 10000 steps, and 10000 options at 1000 steps.

| Set | Steps | Option | Largest | Average | 99% |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Grid | 1,000 | Call | 7.85e-3 | 1.38e-3 | 7.22e-3 |
| Grid | 1,000 | Put | 7.68e-3 | 1.24e-3 | 4.79e-3 |
| Grid | 10,000 | Call | 7.85e-4 | 1.46e-4 | 7.22e-4 |
| Grid | 10,000 | Put | 7.68e-4 | 1.34e-4 | 6.27e-4 |
| Random | 1,000 | Call | 7.98e-3 | 1.86e-3 | 5.76e-3 |
| Random | 1,000 | Put | 7.21e-3 | 1.90e-3 | 5.74e-3 |

The results show same convergence as for European options (study B). The worst errors were observed on the most expensive options (call 38.6, put 35.5), so relative error is small (under 0.03%). The worst call has b = r = 0.05 meaning no dividends, and its error matches study B exactly, since in this case exercising is never optimal.

Pricing a set of 10000 random options took 4345ms for call options and 4366ms for put options, which comes down to 0.4345ms per call option and 0.4366ms per put option (Release build, Apple M4).

## E. No-arbitrage rules

5 no-arbitrage rules were checked for American and European prices using binomial lattice with the same number of steps to ensure that both sides share the same error.

| Rule | Checked | Violations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| American call ≥ European call | 180 | 0 |
| American put ≥ European put | 180 | 0 |
| American call ≥ intrinsic value | 180 | 0 |
| American put ≥ intrinsic value | 180 | 0 |
| American call = European call when b ≥ r | 60 | 0 |

## F. Convergence of long-maturity American option price to perpetual

Long-maturity American price was compared to perpetual American price across maturity from 1 year to 100 years using 100 steps per year. Library's own code for analytic solution was used for benchmark since it shares no code with American options.

| T (years) | Call | Gap | Put | Gap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 11.667 | 6.84 | 0.627 | 2.40 |
| 2 | 13.099 | 5.40 | 1.264 | 1.77 |
| 5 | 15.612 | 2.89 | 2.220 | 0.811 |
| 10 | 17.345 | 1.16 | 2.748 | 0.283 |
| 20 | 18.274 | 0.230 | 2.981 | 0.0501 |
| 30 | 18.448 | 0.0551 | 3.019 | 0.0123 |
| 50 | 18.496 | 7.2e-3 | 3.028 | 2.9e-3 |
| 100 | 18.499 | 4.1e-3 | 3.029 | 2.3e-3 |

The results show clear convergence of American option and perpetual American option. The gap between two is always positive as a finite option can never be worth more than the perpetual one. The gap flattens after T = 50 due to error coming from binomial lattice.

## G. American vega and theta: bump size

Vega and theta for American (1000 steps) at-the-money call option computed using divided differences method was compared to analytic solution of the same European option (since b = r, call price is the same).

| Bump | Vega error | Theta error |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.1 | −9.09e-2 | −6.21e-3 |
| 0.01 | −1.02e-2 | +1.35e-3 |
| 0.001 | −9.49e-3 | +1.42e-3 |
| 1e-4 | −9.49e-3 | +1.43e-3 |
| 1e-5 | −9.49e-3 | +1.43e-3 |
| 1e-6 | −9.49e-3 | +1.43e-3 |

The result shows that bump size of 1e-4 is optimal, as for smaller bump-size the error comes mostly from price error of a binomial lattice. Therefore, bump size  of 1e-4 is used by default in the library.

## Test suite

`test.cpp` runs 257 checks, all passing. They cover the European, perpetual and American option classes, as well as matrix pricer and binomial engine class templates: prices and sensitivities against reference values, construction, copying, the binomial engine, grids, CSV input and output, other functionality and exception handling.
